institutional_shifts: DOJ: transformed this week from an independent prosecutorial body into an instrument of presidential will, with the removal of a career U.S. Attorney and installation of a loyalist who produced an indictment against a political critic within days.
Executive branch: issued two major unilateral directives (Antifa terrorist designation, NSPM-7 domestic terrorism memo) expanding investigatory reach over civil society without congressional input.

Media/regulatory agencies: FCC chair's public pressure campaign against a broadcaster demonstrates regulatory capture being used as a censorship lever; some corporate capitulation (Sinclair) and some resistance (Kimmel's return, journalist letters).

Judiciary: mixed signals—lower courts continued blocking administration policies (UCLA funding, grant conditions) while SCOTUS allowed removal of an independent FTC commissioner, chipping at agency independence precedent.

States/Congress: state health alliances and legislatures (California, Northeast/West Coast coalitions) asserted independent authority against federal health guidance; House Democrats and a handful of Republicans registered public alarm, but GOP leadership blocked oversight (Epstein files, bank subpoenas).
oddities_or_open_questions: The 'UN escalator sabotage' episode—where Trump and the White House alleged deliberate UN staff sabotage despite UN and even Trump's own delegation contradicting the claim—reveals a striking willingness to manufacture grievance narratives at the highest level; worth tracking whether such fabrications become a repeatable governing tactic.

The abrupt, unexplained summons of ~800 senior military generals/admirals to Quantico by Hegseth, with no stated purpose and downplayed by Trump/Vance, is unprecedented and merits close follow-up regarding civil-military relations and possible loyalty-testing intent.

The Treasury's $20B Argentina currency swap, apparently linked to hedge funder Rob Citrone's personal relationship with Bessent and prior insider bond purchases, raises unresolved conflict-of-interest and possible non-public-information questions that warrant financial and ethics investigation.
summary: This was a week of overt weaponization of state power against perceived political enemies, marking one of the starkest escalations yet documented. Trump publicly and repeatedly demanded DOJ prosecutions of Comey, James, and Schiff; fired a US Attorney who found insufficient evidence; installed an inexperienced personal loyalist (Halligan) who then obtained a grand jury indictment of Comey within days. Simultaneously, the administration signed sweeping executive actions designating Antifa a domestic terrorist organization and issuing NSPM-7, a memorandum granting law enforcement broad authority to investigate left-leaning nonprofits and activists. Media capture intensified via FCC pressure on ABC/Kimmel, Sinclair's propagandistic Kirk special, and continued affiliate suppression. A bribery investigation into border czar Homan was closed by Trump appointees and then denied by the White House despite documentary evidence. Foreign policy saw erratic tariff threats, an opaque Argentina bailout benefiting a Bessent associate, and sanctions against a Brazilian judge's family. Courts, states, and civil society mounted meaningful resistance throughout.
top_themes: Governing by retaliation: direct presidential demands for prosecution of named political opponents (Comey, James, Schiff, Soros) culminating in an indictment obtained by a hand-picked, inexperienced loyalist prosecutor.

Normalization of security-state tools against dissent: Antifa terrorist designation and NSPM-7 memo create legal machinery to investigate civil society, nonprofits, and protest movements under vague domestic-terrorism framing.

Media capture and coercion: FCC threats against ABC, Sinclair's conditional reinstatement demands, and continued affiliate blackouts show regulatory leverage used to punish speech critical of the administration.

Corruption with impunity: the Homan bribery investigation closure, contradictory White House denials despite documented evidence, and the Bessent-linked Argentina bailout illustrate elite protection and self-enrichment patterns.

Institutional hollowing paired with resistance: courts, state legislatures (Northeast/West Coast health alliances, California's mask ban), and career prosecutors pushed back, but were frequently overridden, fired, or ignored.
